Quantitative MRI plus local language models drafts neurodegenerative reports

In 192 ADNI cases, an automated MRI-to-report pipeline achieved 77.6%-97.9% accuracy for CSF-space findings and 91.7%-97.4% agreement within one grade on ordinal visual scales, but strict scale agreement was only 27.1%-57.8% and no clinical utility was tested.

Key quantitative results: Accuracy for CSF-space analysis ranged from 77.6% to 97.9% across findings.

BiomarkersMRIBrain atrophyWhite matter hyperintensitiesImaging interpretation

Added October 14, 2026 · DOI:10.1016/j.acra.2026.09.056; PMID:42864178

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The study separates quantitative extraction from narrative drafting and shows where each fails. CSF-space findings and one-grade-tolerant ordinal ratings were often close to neuroradiologist reports, but exact ordinal agreement was poor and model-specific omissions, additions and numeric errors persisted. This is feasibility evidence for reporting assistance, not validation for diagnosis, treatment eligibility or unsupervised use.

Study design

Investigators randomly selected 192 ADNI participants with 3D T1 and 2D or 3D FLAIR MRI. A deep-learning quantitative MRI system generated structured findings for nine indices covering atrophy, white matter hyperintensities and CSF-space abnormalities, which were compared with neuroradiologist reference reports. Four locally deployable language models—GPT-OSS 20B, MedGemma 4B, Phi-3 and Llama 3.1 8B—then drafted clinician-facing conclusions. Reviewers scored accuracy, relevance, clarity and satisfaction on five-point scales and categorized language, omission, addition and numeric errors.

Key quantitative results

  • Accuracy for CSF-space analysis ranged from 77.6% to 97.9% across findings.
  • For ordinal visual scales, strict agreement with reference reports was 27.1%-57.8%; allowing a one-grade difference increased agreement to 91.7%-97.4%.
  • GPT-OSS 20B achieved median Likert scores of 5 across most report-quality metrics and the lowest output-error rates. Phi-3 and Llama 3.1 8B had more language, omission and addition errors, while MedGemma had the highest numeric-error rate.
  • The study reported no prospective effect on neuroradiologist efficiency, diagnostic accuracy, downstream management or patient outcomes.

What changed

A new end-to-end evaluation quantifies both imaging-marker extraction and language-model drafting errors, providing a more operational test of automated neurodegenerative MRI reporting than standalone image-classification or text-generation studies.

Strength of evidence

Early technical feasibility evidence from a modest, retrospectively selected ADNI sample with neuroradiologist reports as the reference. The study does not establish analytical validity across scanners and sites, clinical validity against pathology or outcomes, or clinical utility in a prospective reporting workflow.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The pipeline may support structured drafting under neuroradiologist supervision, but low strict agreement on ordinal scales and model-specific numeric or content errors preclude autonomous interpretation. It should not be used to confirm Alzheimer pathology, stage disease or determine disease-modifying treatment eligibility without validated clinical review.

Field medical relevance

Relevant to biomarker implementation, radiology workflow design and MSL questions about how quantitative imaging and generative AI might standardize reporting while preserving human oversight.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Performance depended on the reporting component: GPT-OSS 20B achieved the highest overall ratings and lowest error rates, while smaller models produced more language, omission and addition errors and MedGemma had the highest numeric-error rate. The study did not validate interchangeability across models or scanners.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No availability, authorization, reimbursement or coverage change. Local language models could eventually reduce data-transfer barriers, but the study did not evaluate deployment cost, integration, governance, cybersecurity or access in routine practice.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Did the system match neuroradiologists exactly?
Not reliably for ordinal scales: strict agreement was 27.1%-57.8%. Agreement exceeded 91% only when a one-grade difference was accepted.
Was clinical utility demonstrated?
No. The study did not prospectively test report turnaround, diagnostic decisions, treatment selection, clinician behavior or patient outcomes.
Is the pipeline authorized for clinical use?
No authorization, guideline endorsement, availability or coverage was established in the report.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Retrospective sample of 192 ADNI participants
  • Reference was clinical reporting rather than pathology or an external outcome
  • Low strict agreement for ordinal visual scales
  • No external multi-site or scanner validation reported
  • Model-specific omissions, additions, language errors and numeric errors
  • No prospective workflow, clinical-utility or patient-outcome evaluation

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record

Ko JS, Jung W, Suh PS, et al. Automated Structured Reporting of Neurodegenerative Imaging Markers Using Quantitative MRI and Large Language Models. Acad Radiol. Published online October 13, 2026. doi:10.1016/j.acra.2026.09.056.
